Multiple Endovascular Devices) meta-­ analysis. 9 Under these circumstances, HERMES showed better clinical outcomes in reperfused patients with ASPECTS 0-5 than non-­ reperfused patients.

To date, a smaller body of literature has conducted a long-­ term assessment of expected health benefits and costs associated with AIS patients with large core infarctions. 10-12 Using data from the HERMES meta-­ analysis, Wu et al found that EVT is more cost-­ effective than medical care alone, and Khunte et al stated that EVT yields higher quality-­ adjusted life years (QALYs) regardless of the quality of collateral circulation. 11 12 However, previous cost-­ effectiveness analyses used data from trials that were not designed to select low ASPECTS patients. In this study, we incorporated modified Rankin Scale (mRS)-­ based outcomes specific to patients presenting with low ASPECTS. We hypothesized that EVT in AIS patients with ASPECTS 3-5 would be cost-­ effective given the improved clinical outcomes compared with standard care (SC) alone. This study aimed to conduct a decision-­ analytical model to assess the effectiveness of EVT, compared with SC alone, in AIS patients with a large ischemic region over their lifetime.

A decision-­ analytic model was developed in Tree Age Pro 2022 software (TreeAge Software, Williamstown, MA) to evaluate the cost-­ effectiveness of EVT compared with SC alone from a healthcare perspective in the USA. The model was designed to assess AIS patients presenting with an ASPECTS of 3 to 5 between 0 and 24 hours after stroke symptom onset. In the base-­ case scenario the average age of the modeled cohort was 76 years old in accordance with the average age of patients in the RESCUE-­ Japan LIMIT. 8 Institutional review board approval was not required for this study as input parameters for the decision-­ analytic model were derived from published sources.

The two clinical care pathways analyzed for comparison were EVT with SC, and SC alone. In order to preserve consistency with real-­ life clinical scenarios and published sources such as the RESCUE-­ Japan LIMIT, patients with a confirmed large vessel occlusion and ASPECTS 3-5 received SC, including intravenous tissue-­ plasminogen activator (IV-­ tPA) thrombolysis (if eligible) in both strategies. After each treatment strategy, patients were categorized into one of seven mutually exclusive health states according to the degree of dependence on daily activities as defined by the mRS score 90 days after hospital discharge. The mRS score was categorized as 0 (no disability) to 5 (severe disability), and 6 (death) (table 1)

A long-­ term Markov state transition model was built to estimate lifetime health benefits and costs at the end of the acute care pathway. We assumed the model would be repeated using a 1 year cycle length until all patients expired to reflect the lifetime horizon. Patients could remain in the same mRS state during each cycle, experience a recurrent stroke, or die. 13 Patients who stay in the same mRS state incur the mRS-­ based chronic care cost assigned to that health state. Patients who experience a recurrent stroke could either recover or die. Those who recover transition to a worse mRS state, incurring a combined cost including recurrent stroke care costs and mRS-­ based chronic care costs. Given an increased risk of mortality among patients with worse mRS outcomes (mRS 3-5), mRS-­ based hazard ratios (table 1) were also incorporated into the model. 14 15 Furthermore, the age-­ related risk for non-­ stroke mortality causes for the general population was derived from the 2019 United States Life Tables. 16

The complete structure of the decision tree is detailed in figure 1.

All input parameters were derived from the best available evidence in the literature, represented by RCTs, meta-­ analyses, or large-­ cohort studies. The 90-­ day mRS outcomes were obtained from the most recent RCT by Yoshimura et al . The cost of EVT and IV-­ tPA was derived from a study by Kuntz et al who obtained the costs from the National Inpatient Sample. 17
Figure 1 Structure of decision tree: short-­ term model and long-­ term model. EVT, endovascular thrombectomy; mRS, modified Rankin Scale; SC, standard care.

Acute care costs, chronic care costs, and recurrent stroke costs were also derived from Kunz et al, which extracted the costs from Dawson et al, Shireman et al and Chambers et al , respectively. 17-20 All costs were inflation-­ adjusted to 2021 US$ using the medical care consumer price index (US Bureau of Labor Statistics). 21 The mRS-­ based utility was derived from Peultier et al who estimated a weighted utility for each mRS outcome. 14 An annual discount rate of 3% was applied to the mRS-­ based utility and costs per convention.
A list of all input parameters is detailed in table 1.

The incremental cost-­ effectiveness ratio (ICER) was assessed by using a willingness-­ to-­ pay (WTP) threshold of $100 000 per QALY, following the US guideline recommendations. 22 Sensitivity analyses were performed to explore the robustness and accuracy of the model. Thus, deterministic one-­ way and two-­ way sensitivity analyses were performed to identify and evaluate the key variables driving the model and assess the effect of uncertainties on one (two) input parameter(s) on the results. Another indicator used to compare strategies was the net monetary benefit (NMB).

Probabilistic sensitivity analyses (PSAs) were performed to assess the robustness of the model results. PSA was conducted using 10 000 iterations of a Monte Carlo simulation by varying input parameters values from their respective distributions (table 1). Results were described using a cost-­ effectiveness scatterplot and cost-­ effectiveness acceptability curves.

We performed the following validation of our decision model according to best practices. 23 24 (1) Face validation : acute stroke clinicians vetted the model structure, input values, and results against their clinical expertise. (2) Verification analyses : we validated that the results are independent of the model structure. For the EVT strategy, an increase of the probabilities for the mRS states 0 and 1 led to higher effectiveness and lower cost of the EVT treatment over a lifetime horizon. For the SC strategy, a decrease of the probability for the mRS state 6 led to higher effectiveness and higher cost of the SC treatment over a lifetime horizon. These results are consistent with our expectations given the model structure.

The cost-­ effectiveness analyses revealed that EVT yields higher lifetime benefits (2.20 QALYs vs 1.41 QALYs) with higher lifetime healthcare cost per patient ($285 861 vs $272 954), compared with the SC strategy. The difference in health benefits between EVT and SC was 0.79 QALYs, equivalent to 288 additional days of healthy life per patient. Thus, EVT is more effective and costly compared with SC alone, representing an undominated strategy. However, EVT is still cost-­ effective since the ICER of $16 239/QALY is lower than the WTP thresholds of 50 000/QALY and 100 000/QALY. The NMBs were negative for EVT and SC strategies.

The results of the tornado diagram (online supplemental figure S1) showed that the ICER is most sensitive to: (1) stroke related-­ mortality risk after each type of treatment strategies (EVT and SC); (2) age; (3) proportion of good outcomes (mRS 2) after SC and EVT; and (4) poor outcomes (mRS 3) after EVT.

(C) Two-­ way sensitivity analyses varying mortality risks of EVT and SC. (D) Two-­ way sensitivity analyses varying mortality risk of EVT and probability of excellent outcome after SC (mRS score of 0). In the blue region, EVT is more cost-­ effective whereas in the red region SC is more cost-­ effective. The dashed line represents the base-­ case scenario. EVT, endovascular thrombectomy treatment; mRS, modified Rankin Scale; SC, standard care.

The mortality risk of each strategy was varied independently. When the mortality risk after EVT varies within a plausible range, EVT remains the preferred strategy (figure 2A). Likewise, EVT is more favorable when the mortality risk after SC varies from 0% to 30% (figure 2B). T wo-­ way sensitivity analyses were performed, simultaneously varying the mortality risk of EVT and SC from 0% to 30%. The results indicated that EVT was the optimal strategy throughout this range (figure 2C). When the proportion of excellent outcomes (mRS 0) after SC varies from 0% to 20% and mortality risk of EVT varies from 0% to 30%, the results indicated that EVT was cost-­ effective if excellent outcomes (mRS 0) after SC were at most 5.5% (figure 2D).

Additional one-­ way sensitivity analysis varying patient age from 50 to 100 showed that NMBs were negative for both strategies throughout this age range (online supplemental figure S2A). However, EVT remained the most cost-­ effective strategy until age 97.9 years. The difference between the NMB of EVT and SC became smaller with the advancement of age, mainly because benefits and costs were higher in younger patients than in older patients. T wo-­ way sensitivity analyses demonstrated that EVT was the most cost-­ effective strategy until age 98 as long as the proportion of excellent outcomes (mRS 0) of SC is lower than 10% (online supplemental figure S2B). When varying the patient age from 50 to 100 and the mortality risk of EVT from 0% to 30%, the conclusions of the base-­ case scenario remained unchanged until age 97 (online supplemental figure S2C). Furthermore, EVT was the most cost-­ effective strategy until age 92 when varying the patient age from 50 to 100 years old, and the proportion of good outcomes (mRS 0) (online supplemental figure S2D) and poor outcomes (mRS 3) after EVT from 0% to 20% (online supplemental figure S2E).

The probabilistic sensitivity analyses in the base-­ case scenario for 76-­ year-­ old patients with ASPECTS 3-5 indicated that EVT was the more cost-­ effective strategy in 98.8% (9882 of 10 000) of iterations at the WTP threshold of $100 000 per QALY (figure 3A). The cost-­ effectiveness acceptability curves varying the WTP thresholds from $0 to $200 000 showed that EVT was the optimal strategy for almost all WTP thresholds. Notably, a higher WTP threshold led to a higher number of iterations where EVT was more favorable (figure 3B).

The total dots below the dashed threshold line representing willingness-­ to-­ pay (WTP) (green dots) denote the probability of endovascular thrombectomy treatment being more cost-­ effective. This study examined the cost-­ effectiveness of EVT in suspected AIS patients with a large ischemic core, defined as ASPECTS 3-5. The analysis found that EVT is a cost-­ effective strategy compared with SC alone over the patient's lifetime. Despite higher initial costs with EVT, this strategy yielded higher QALYs with an ICER lower than the WTP thresholds of $50 000/QALY and $100 000/ QALY. The AHA and American College of Cardiology (ACC) recommend high-­ value care when cost-­ effectiveness levels are reached with ICERs below $50 000/QALY, and intermediate value of care with ICERs between $50 000/QALY and $150 000/ QALY. Per the AHA/ACC policy statement, EVT provides high-­ value care in AIS patients with a large ischemic core compared with SC alone. 25 The PSA results showed that EVT was the most cost-­ effective strategy at all levels of WTP thresholds, ranging from $0 to $200 000 per QALY.

Current guidelines from the AHA/ASA recommend EVT only in patients with ASPECTS ≥6. 5 However, the range of ASPECTS values is not an exact quantification of the infarct volume, 8 and the likelihood of good outcomes is not homogeneous throughout the scale. For instance, Panni et al found that patients with ASPECTS 5 had a 37.5% chance of good outcomes (mRS 0-2), while none of the patients with ASPECTS 0-1 had good outcomes after EVT. 26 One study by Roman et al found that ASPECTS 0-2 patients had an 11% probability of good outcomes (mRS 0-2) after EVT, while it was 15% for patients with ASPECTS 3-5. 27 Another study by Cagnazzo et al documented that patients presenting with ASPECTS 5 who underwent EVT had a higher probability of good outcomes (mRS 0-2) (33.3%) than ASPECTS 0-4 patients (17.1%). 28 Even though Yoshimura et al only included ASPECTS 3-5 patients, current evidence has shown that this sub-­ group of all low-­ ASPECTS patients would benefit the most from EVT. 8 Moreover, our results revealed that it is also the most cost-­ effective strategy compared with SC alone in the long term (lifetime horizon).

Furthermore, national guidelines from the AHA/ASA advise performing EVT on AIS patients aged 18 and older without an upper age limit, 5 and evidence from RCTs supports this class I recommendation. 1-4 6 For instance, the HERMES meta-­ analysis documented that EVT was associated with improved functional outcomes within 12 hours of symptom onset compared with SC alone among patients ≥80 years old. 9 Similarly, the DAWN (DWI or CTP Assessment with Clinical Mismatch in the Triage of Wake-­ Up and Late Presenting Strokes Undergoing Neurointervention with Trevo) trial showed that EVT had more favorable outcomes than SC among elderly patients (≥80) in the extended time window (6-24 hours of symptom onset). 29 However, there is a lack of consensus about the effectiveness of EVT in older patients presenting with ASPECTS ≥6. Prior research docu -mented that the effectiveness of EVT in patients above 80 years of age depends significantly on the morbidity of the patients at baseline. 30 In contrast, one study found that EVT is the preferred strategy over SC in patients aged 50 to 100 years. 17 Another study indicated that EVT yielded higher QALYs and incremental costs compared with SC alone, but EVT was still cost-­ effective in patients aged 76-80. 20 Even though further research is required to understand the effectiveness of EVT in low ASPECTS patients aged ≥80, Wu et al demonstrated that EVT was cost-­ effective in older (≥75 years) and younger (55-65, 65-75 years) patients presenting with ASPECTS <6. 11 Our results are consistent with the most recent cost-­ effectiveness evidence suggesting that EVT improves health outcomes in patients aged 50 to 98.6 years presenting with ASPECTS 3-5.

This study has several strengths. The outcome parameters were derived from the first and most recent RCT data incorporating mRS-­ based outcomes specific to patients presenting with low ASPECTS. Further, sensitivity analyses were performed to explore the robustness and accuracy of the model. Additionally, our model is flexible and can be used with data from ongoing clinical trials (eg, TESLA: Thrombectomy for Emergent Salvage of Large Anterior Circulation Ischemic Stroke; TENSION: Efficacy and Safety of Thrombectomy in Stroke with Extended Lesion and Extended Time Window) once their results are released. However, there are also limitations in this study. Due to the lack of availability of input parameters, subgroup analyses were not performed. Yet, extensive sensitivity analyses of input parameters were conducted to address this concern. Even though EVT was associated with an increased incidence of sICH, sensitivity analysis could not be performed on this important variable due to the lack of mRS outcomes in patients who had sICH. More research is needed to determine the clinical implications of a higher incidence of sICH among low ASPECTS patients. Finally, mRS outcomes are based on a Japanese study since US-­ specific data are not available yet. Therefore, sensitivity analysis was performed to evaluate the robustness of the model, and the conclusions remain unchanged within plausible ranges.

Our study highlights that EVT is cost-­ effective for AIS patients with a large ischemic core, defined as ASPECTS 3-5, over a lifetime horizon. Moreover, EVT is associated with a significant improvement in clinical outcomes of patients aged 50 to 98 years. Further studies are needed to elucidate the clinical implications of a higher incidence of sICH among low ASPECTS patients.

Sarraj A, Hassan AE, Abraham MG, et al; SELECT2 Investigators. Trial of endovascular thrombectomy for large ischemic strokes. N Engl J Med. 2023;388:1259-1271.

Question: In patients with acute ischemic stroke with a large ischemic-core volume, what is the effect of endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) within 24 hours of stroke onset added to standard medical therapy vs. standard medical therapy alone on functional outcomes?
Design: Randomized controlled trial (SELECT2 [Randomized Controlled Trial to Optimize Patient's Selection for Endovascular Treatment in Acute Ischemic Stroke]). Trial was stopped early for efficacy.
Blinding: Treatment allocation concealed; blinded (data collectors and 90-day outcome assessors).*
Setting: 31 sites in Australia, Canada, Europe, New Zealand, and USA.
Patients: 352 patients aged 18 to 85 years (median age, 67 y; 59% men; median Alberta Stroke Program Early Computed Tomography Score

[ASPECTS], 4) who had acute ischemic stroke due to occlusion of the internal carotid artery (cervical or intracranial) or the M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery or both, with a large ischemic core on noncontrast computed tomography (CT) (ASPECTS value = 3 to 5; score range, 0 to 10; lower value = larger infarction) or estimated ischemic-core volume ≥ 50 mL on CT perfusion imaging, prestroke modified Rankin scale (mRs) score of 0 to 1 (no disability), and no evidence of intracranial hemorrhage.
Interventions: EVT plus standard medical therapy according to local protocols and international guidelines ( n = 178) or standard medical therapy alone ( n = 174).
*See Glossary. Some information provided by authors.
Results : EVT plus standard medical therapy vs. standard medical therapy alone in acute ischemic stroke with a large ischemiccore volume (intention-to-treat analysis)

Commentary: EVT is currently recommended for acute ischemic stroke in patients presenting ≤ 24 hours from symptom onset with large-vessel occlusion and small ischemic core volume (ASPECTS ≥ 6 and National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale disability score ≥ 6) (1). The SELECT2 trial evaluated whether EVT in patients with large ischemic-core volume leads to better functional outcomes than standard medical therapy alone, including IV thrombolytics for those who were eligible.

The SELECT2 trial included only patients with excellent baseline function (i.e., mRs of 0 or 1). Overall, 20% of patients in the EVT group achieved functional independence at 90 days compared with 7% in the medical therapy group. Of note, 18.5% of patients in the EVT group had procedural complications, including arterial access-site complications (hematoma and infection), vascular dissection, arterial perforation, and intraprocedural vasospasm.

The focus on pragmatic outcomes, including functional independence, procedural complications, and quality of life, is a strength of the trial. A major limitation is that it was stopped early, which introduces bias and possibly overestimates the treatment effect.
A growing body of evidence shows improved function with EVT for acute ischemic stroke with large ischemic burden (2). The SELECT2 trial supports considering

abstract: While imaging has traditionally played a fundamental role in the selection of patients undergoing endovascular thrombectomy, recent thrombectomy trials involving patients with large ischemic strokes demonstrated a consistent benefit of endovascular thrombectomy across all imaging strata, suggesting that reperfusion benefit may exist independent of current imaging constructs. Although these findings attest to the uniformly beneficial effects of reperfusion, they also shed doubt on the accuracy and utility of our imaging modalities in defining reversible versus irreversible ischemia and challenge the premise of imaging-based selection. We aimed to review the histopathologic studies and clinical trials that have shaped our understanding of current imaging constructs aiming to outline the existing imaging-neuropathological gap that may be far wider than previously perceived.

The Imaging-Neuropathological Gap in Acute Large Vessel Occlusive Stroke
Ahmad A. Ballout , MD; David S. Liebeskind , MD; Tudor G. Jovin , MD; Souhel Najjar , MD

While imaging has traditionally played a fundamental role in the selection of patients undergoing endovascular thrombectomy, recent thrombectomy trials involving patients with large ischemic strokes demonstrated a consistent benefit of endovascular thrombectomy across all imaging strata, suggesting that reperfusion benefit may exist independent of current imaging constructs. Although these findings attest to the uniformly beneficial effects of reperfusion, they also shed doubt on the accuracy and utility of our imaging modalities in defining reversible versus irreversible ischemia and challenge the premise of imaging-based selection. We aimed to review the histopathologic studies and clinical trials that have shaped our understanding of current imaging constructs aiming to outline the existing imaging-neuropathological gap that may be far wider than previously perceived.

Key Words: brain ◼ brain ischemia ◼ infarction ◼ ischemic stroke ◼ magnetic resonance imaging

I maging-based selection for the endovascular treatment of large vessel ischemic stroke has been premised on imaging constructs of the core and penumbra. These entities were first postulated from early animal studies and later refined in humans using various hemodynamic, metabolic, and noninvasive imaging models. 1,2 Enthusiasm surrounded these constructs after studies suggested that these concepts may have the capability of ascertaining the degree of clinical benefit derived from reperfusion. 3 Momentum was later gained following a wave of positive endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) trials for which imaging-based selection was believed to play a pivotal role in the trials' success. 4,5 The recent large-core trials, however, have challenged the accuracy of these constructs and the very premise of imaging-based selection, as these studies have suggested that the benefit of EVT may exist independent of core size or penumbral volume. 6-13 While these findings may testify to the power of the treatment, they equally contest the accuracy of our imaging constructs in predicting the viability of tissue and their clinical utility in determining the extent of clinical benefit of reperfusion. 12,13 Indeed, the imagingneuropathological gap inherent to our imaging may be far wider than we had previously perceived. Our aim was to review the histopathologic studies and clinical trials that have shaped our understanding of core and penumbra as a preliminary step to hopefully narrow the imaging-neuropathological gap.
DEFINING THE ISCHEMIC CORE AND PENUMBRA

The ischemic core represents hypoperfused brain regions that have undergone morphologically irreversible damage (infarction), while the penumbra represents functionally impaired but salvageable tissue. 1,2 Although the penumbra is an elusive phenomenon that is in constant flux between its recruitment into the core and its escape into a band of oligemia, 1 our operational models have reduced it to a static definition usually based on a snapshot in time of computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) derived thresholds that attempt to delimit these imaginary boundaries. 14,15 These transition zones are based on animal and human studies that have largely used quantitative hemodynamics, molecular, and noninvasive imaging to define them.

Hemodynamic definitions derived primarily from positron emission tomography studies have estimated that cerebral infarction (core) occurs at cerebral blood flow (CBF) of <10 mL/100 g, functionally impaired but salvageable tissue (penumbra) occurs between CBF levels of 10 to 20 mL/100 g, and hypoperfused but not imminently at-risk tissue (noncore nonpenumbra) exists between CBF levels of 20 to 30 mL/100 g. 16-18 Molecular definitions of the ischemic core and penumbra have focused on protein synthesis, ATP production, and HSP (heat-shock protein) induction. A decrease in protein synthesis occurs when the relative CBF value drops to 30% to 50% of baseline, potentially reversible with ATP preservation (penumbra) but leading to irreversible translation blockade and infarction (core) with complete ATP loss. 2,18,19 HSP70 (heat shock protein 70), crucial for protein repair, is expressed postischemia, but only regions with adequate energy reserves can translate it into functional protein, suggesting potential recovery. Given the differential ischemic vulnerabilities between cell lines, 20 a tissue sample may exhibit heterogeneous infarction patterns due to variations in various energy reserves and protein synthesis capabilities (Figure 1).

The spatial resolution of diffusion MRI limits its capability to directly analyze morphological changes that occur on a cellular level. Therefore, the viability of tissue can only be inferred based on previous histopathologic correlations. We will analyze the literature to assess the evidence that supports or negates the hypothesis that diffusion restriction, or specific apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) thresholds, can be used to predict irreversible infarction.

The quality of evidence supporting the correlation between diffusion restriction and histopathologic infarction was assessed in a systemic review of focal ischemic stroke models using a predefined methodological quality scoring system. 21 Of the 1579 papers screened, 141 met inclusion for review, with only 13 (9.7%) meeting their prespecified quality threshold, and only 3 studies (2% of total animals) had performed blinded analyses. Less than a quarter of studies quantified the correlation between diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and histological analysis beyond stating that they correlated well and only 13% examined subregions of the DWI lesion or histopathologic abnormality. We examined the 13 studies in detail (Table S1), 22-34 among others, 35-39
and distilled the key takeaway points pertinent to the hypothesis.

In the absence of reperfusion, specific ADC thresholds can approximate the macroscopically visible boundaries of stained tissue infarction, but heterogeneous ADC values likely exist within these boundaries, suggesting spatial variance in energy failure across the demarcated area.

In 1990, Moseley et al 35,36 conducted 2 studies involving permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) showing a close correlation between the diffusionrestricted and histopathologic volumes at 24 hours. Subsequent studies of permanent MCAO found significant heterogeneity of ADC existing within the histopathologic margins of infarction. 37,38

Before reperfusion, the DWI region appears to approximate the macroscopically visible boundaries of stained tissue infarction with relative accuracy. Overestimation may occur with ultraearly reperfusion, while slight underestimation or overestimation may occur with delayed reperfusion.

In a temporary MCAO model, transient ischemia of <20 minutes did not result in any apparent changes in ADC or histopathology, suggesting that ultraearly reperfusion may prevent histopathologic damage. 39 In a study involving 45 minutes of transient MCAO, DWI lesions underestimated infarction margins by 6%, 30 contrasted by another study demonstrating a 6% overestimation of the infarction margins when reperfusion occurred within 120 minutes. 34 Another study showed less than a 15% volume difference between the DWI estimated and histopathologic infarction margins but did not specify whether this difference resulted from underestimation or overestimation. 24

Discordance may exist between the ADC signal intensity, the extent of histopathologic injury, and functional outcomes. Regional variability of the ADC value may exist transiently but is rapidly abolished and may not necessarily correlate with the degree of histopathologic injury.

In a study of rats undergoing transient MCAO for 30 minutes, investigators found a 5× greater proportion of neuronal necrosis in the striatum compared with the cortex, despite similar ADC values between regions, with complete functional recovery in all rats. 26 Conversely, in a study of permanent MCAO for 90 minutes, a higher proportion of shrunken neurons were found in the cortex compared with the striatum, despite the cortex exhibiting nearly half of the ADC decrease. 29 Regional ADC variability was found between cortical and striatal regions following 36 minutes of MCAO, but levels became comparable after 48 minutes of ischemia, highlighting the short-lived ADC variability that may exist. 29
ADC normalization, whether transient (pseudonormalization) or persistent, cannot reliably be used to predict histopathologic recovery.

Following rapid reperfusion, ADC normalization can either persist or result in a secondary decline several hours after reperfusion (pseudonormalization). 26,28,32 Notably, both neuronal and astrocytic injuries appear to progress despite transient or persistent ADC normalization, and the extent of injury does not seem to temporally align with the ADC value. 26,27 Compared with secondary ADC decline, persistent ADC normalization may be associated with less neurological injury; however, significant neuronal injury may still be identified by using immunohistochemical stains, such as MAP2 (microtubuleassociated protein 2), which may be missed on macroscopic histopathologic stains. 28,32

There is likely a link between neuronal shrinkage and astroglia swelling that exists during acute ischemia. The initial ADC decline may indicate astroglia swelling as a compensatory response to neuronal shrinkage, while ADC normalization could signal a temporary balance occurring post-reperfusion. The secondary decline in ADC may reflect compensatory failure, resulting in recurrent glial swelling or disintegration (Figure 2).

Multiple studies consistently show astroglia swelling alongside neuronal shrinkage during ischemia or reperfusion. 25,27,29,32 For instance, Ringer et al 32 investigated immunohistopathological changes during transient ischemia lasting 30 minutes. They found partial or complete DWI reversal in all 11 rats within 5 hours, with recurrence at 24 hours, indicating DWI pseudonormalization. Despite reversed DWI signals, significant loss of neuronal MAP2 was observed, affecting about a third of the initial DWI lesion. HSP72 signaling, a neuroprotectant indicative of ischemic stress, 19 persisted in the reversed DWI region. In addition, GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein) staining revealed astroglia reactivity and swelling in DWI lesions, which normalized alongside diffusion reversal, illustrating the crucial osmoregulatory role of astroglia during cerebral perfusion compromise. 40
The morphological extent of cell injury depends on the duration of ischemia, although heterogeneous patterns of injury may exist for any given time.

In the acute stage of ischemia, neuronal cell bodies may seem shrunken and triangular, along with neuronal perikarya surrounded by vacuoles. 24 These features may become intermixed with cytoplasmic eosinophilia (red neurons) in the subacute stage, characteristics of delayed neuronal injury. Heterogeneous morphological features may become evident in the chronic stage, such as the abundance of ghost neurons in some tissues, with progression to pan-necrosis in others. This time dependence was further shown in a study demonstrating necrosis in 95% of neurons following 30 minutes of ischemia, while only 17% of neurons were deemed necrotic after 10 minutes of ischemia. 28

Given the absence of human studies directly correlating MRI and histopathology during acute ischemic stroke, the translational use of MRI in acute ischemic stroke has been largely founded on the animal studies above, as well as the clinical, hemodynamic, and radiographic validation following reperfusion. 41 This has largely been premised on the reversibility of DWI and the correlation between initial DWI and final T2 volume. An ADC threshold of <620×10 -6 mm 2 /s has been identified as the optimal threshold at which restricted diffusion is unlikely to reverse, and this threshold has been used by automated software to define the core in modern reperfusion trials. 42

In an evidence-based systemic review assessing the level of evidence supporting the hypothesis that DWI hyperintensity represents irreversible infarction, DWI reversal was estimated to occur at a mean rate of 24% of patients with great variability of lesion reversal (0%83%). 43 These findings, coupled with the absence of any single tissue-outcome correlation study, merited the lowest possible evidence grade of a D based on the Oxford Center for Evidenced-Based Medicine. Further studies have suggested that ADC coefficient thresholds may not predict the response to acute stroke thrombolysis. 44 The DEFUSE 2 study (MRI Profile and Response to Endovascular Reperfusion) 3 proposed diffusion-perfusion mismatch profiles that could potentially differentiate between effective and ineffective reperfusion and was later adopted as inclusion criteria in many contemporary EVT trials. 5 While these target mismatch profiles seem to be Several hours following reperfusion, ADC levels normalize, likely representing a transient state of homeostasis where the astroglia have returned to their near-baseline morphological state. Secondary ADC decline subsequently ensues likely due to secondary energy failure, leading to neuronal and astroglia swelling and disintegration.

strong prognosticators, their ability to predict treatment effect modification following reperfusion remains uncertain and was recently challenged in large-core trials. 7,45

CT-based animal studies focused primarily on how blood flow affects water density and the correlation between x-ray hypoattenuation and final histopathologic volume. Investigators demonstrated that x-ray hypoattenuation likely begins below a critical CBF threshold of 15 to 20 mL/100 g per min, coinciding with the threshold of electrical failure and potential breakdown in synaptic transmission. 46 This occurred above the expected threshold of ionic membrane failure ( ≈ 9-11 mL/100 g per min), suggesting that x-ray hypoattenuation may partially reflect alternative mechanisms that precede ion-pump failure. Another study revealed that the duration of ischemia impacts brain edema development, with cerebral water content increasing from 78% to 80.5% within 3 hours of permanent arterial occlusion and up to 83% within 9 hours. 47 Restoring CBF reduced edema after <1 hour of ischemia but exacerbated it after >3 hours, indicating a critical window for reperfusion effects. 47

Researchers have used CT to measure water content in early ischemic edema. An in vitro model estimated that a 2.6-Houndfields unit decrease in x-ray hypoattenuation likely occurs per 1% increase in water (r=0.992; P <0.0001). 48 A similar relationship was later shown in a rat model undergoing up to 6 hours of MCAO. 49 In this study, a 1% increase in tissue water content correlated with a 1.8-Houndfields unit decrease in attenuation (r=0.55; P <0.001). 49 A study that induced severe focal ischemia in nonhuman primates for 6 hours showed that CT density changes decrease immediately following occlusion, followed by a transient return to normal within 30 to 60 minutes, followed by a secondary decrease beginning at 2 hours and plateauing as it reaches 6 hours. 50 These findings suggested that CT density changes likely lag behind severe focal ischemia by 2 hours. In a reperfusion experiment with rats, x-ray attenuation stabilized after 1 hour of MCAO but steadily decreased after 2 and 4 hours post-reperfusion. 51 In cases where reperfusion occurred after 1 hour, a third of the rats exhibited complete reversal of hypoattenuation with no evidence of macroscopic histopathologic changes. 51 However, histopathologic changes were observed in rats where hypoattenuation either halted or progressed, suggesting that x-ray hypoattenuation may occasionally recover with ultrarapid reperfusion within 1 hour but tends to progress if reperfusion occurs 2 hours or later.

These studies can be summarized with the following statements.
X-ray hypoattenuation likely correlates with CBF below a specific threshold.

X-ray hypoattenuation appears to develop once CBF drops into the band of electrical failure, rather than the expected band of ion-pump failure, suggesting that alternative mechanisms leading to x-ray hypoattenuation may begin before ion-pump failure (Figure 3). 46
Reversal of X-ray hypoattenuation likely correlates with the duration of hypoperfusion.

Ultrarapid reperfusion may lead to the stability, or even the reversal of x-ray hypoattenuation, while delayed reperfusion likely accelerates the rate of x-ray hypoattenuation, suggesting a narrow window in which reperfusion may halt or exacerbate x-ray hypoattenuation. 47
An inverse linear relationship between x-ray hypoattenuation and tissue water likely exists.
A 1% change increase in net water concentration likely correlates with a decrease in x-ray hypoattenuation by ≈ 1.8 to 2.6 Houndfields unit. 48,49
X-ray hypoattenuation may lag severe focal ischemia.
By the time x-ray hypoattenuation is detectable with the naked eye, the ischemic injury is probably 2 hours old. 50

Given the absence of tissue-level validation studies, human studies have relied on radiographic validation of CT hypodensity by comparing the prereperfusion and postreperfusion scans. One of the largest studies investigating the relationship between early ischemic changes and follow-up imaging was performed using the data from the prospective thrombolytic trial, ECASS II (Randomized Double-Blind PlaceboControlled Trial of Thrombolytic Therapy With Intravenous Alteplase in Acute Ischemic Stroke), in patients presenting within 6 hours of symptom onset. 52 In this study, ischemic edema identified on baseline CT was 96% specific for final infarction, and the presence of ischemic edema was a poor prognostic marker. Interestingly, the infarction volume grew by a mean of 13 mL between day 1 and day 7 follow-up scans, despite a 2-point improvement in the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale, highlighting the discrepancy that may exist between volumetric infarction and clinical outcome.
In summary, these studies highlight the connection between x-ray hypoattenuation, the severity and duration of ischemia, and the presence of histopathologic infarction.

The inverse linear relationship between x-ray hypoattenuation and net water concentration allows for noninvasive quantitative measurement of tissue water. However, correlating this with the degree of tissue infarction would require assuming a linear relationship between tissue water and the morphological extent of tissue infarction, for which there is limited evidence. While hypodensity on CT is the lesion least prone to reversibility following reperfusion and may, perhaps, characterize pan-necrosis with the highest specificity, the morphological extent of infarction within a hypodense voxel remains largely unknown. Furthermore, x-ray hypoattenuation likely develops below the threshold of electrical failure, rather than the expected threshold of ion-pump failure, which may, in part, explain the narrow window of potential reversibility of x-ray hypoattenuation (Figure 3). The mechanisms underlying x-ray hypoattenuation that occurs above the threshold of ion-pump failure remain largely unknown. 2 Drawing from the correlative MRI studies above, it seems plausible that this initial decrease in x-ray hypoattenuation could represent, at least in part, a compensatory astroglia response.

Perfusion imaging relies on radiotracers as a blood proxy to quantify hemodynamics and can broadly be categorized based on the permeability of the tracer across the blood-brain barrier. 53 Current technologies use iodine or gadolinium, nondiffusible tracers that are confined to the intravascular space, limiting the hemodynamic outputs to indirect approximations. This differs from diffusible tracers, such as Xenon CT, which freely penetrates tissue allowing for direct, absolute, quantitative hemodynamic measurements. 53 The constraints associated with the insolubility of iodine limit the mathematical calculations of CBF to relative CBF values that depend on contralateral hemispheric flow. 53 Nonetheless, a relative CBF value of <30% (using current nondiffusible tracers) has been shown to be least prone to reversibility, thus, best approximates the infarction volume as assessed on DWI as a reference, and has been used widely in contemporary reperfusion trials. 15 Despite its limitations, including the possibility of core overestimation in early presenting patients, 54 the CBF approximated core has been shown to be a strong predictor of outcome following reperfusion therapy. 45 However, its prognostic value does not equate to treatment effect modification, and in several large-core trials, the CBF-derived estimated infarct volume did not modify the treatment effect of EVT. 12,45,55 The clinical use of CTP will be discussed in the reperfusion trials section below.

Endovascular treatment trials, while primarily addressing reperfusion safety and efficacy, indirectly serve as valuable platforms to assess the accuracy of our imaging modalities in predicting tissue infarction before reperfusion. Our focus will be on discussing the evidence for or against our hypothesis that the benefit of reperfusion may partly exist due to salvageable tissue concealed within the margins of the radiographically estimated core or beyond the penumbra.

The EVT after large vessel ischemic stroke metaanalysis demonstrated a treatment benefit of EVT in early presenting patients with small-to-moderate-sized core volumes, as the participating trials largely excluded patients with the Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score (ASPECTS) of 0 to 5. 4 However, some patients who were enrolled based on local investigator adjudicated ASPECTS scores of >5 were subsequently found by core laboratory review to have lower ASPECTS scores. Subsequent analyses of those patients with core laboratory adjudicated ASPECTS 0 to 5 in EVT after large vessel ischemic stroke revealed a beneficial effect of endovascular therapy compared with standard care. 56 A subsequent meta-analysis revealed that larger ischemic core volumes ( ≥ 70 mL) were independently associated with worse functional outcomes but did not negate the treatment benefit of EVT. 45 Subanalyses of MR CLEAN (A Randomized Trial of Intraarterial Treatment for Acute Ischemic Stroke) 57 and ESCAPE (Randomized Assessment of Rapid Endovascular Treatment of Ischemic Stroke) 55 supported these findings, showing no significant interaction between perfusion core volume (as assessed by CT perfusion) and the treatment effect. In addition, the treatment effect persisted even without a target mismatch profile in the MR CLEAN analysis. 57 The AURORA (Thrombectomy for Anterior Circulation Stroke Beyond 6 h From Time Last Known Well) meta-analysis, 5 like EVT after large vessel ischemic stroke, linked lower baseline ASPECTS scores to less favorable outcomes in late-presenting patients but not necessarily to lack of benefit from EVT. Benefits were comparable between ASPECTS 8 to 10 and ASPECTS 6 to 7 groups, as well as between ASPECTS 8 to 10 and ASPECTS 0 to 7 groups. Firm conclusions for ASPECTS 0 to 5 were hindered by their <10% representation; however, no heterogeneity of treatment effect could be demonstrated when this baseline imaging category was specifically analyzed in subgroup analysis compared with ASPECTS 6 to 7 and 8 to 10.

Five randomized controlled trials unequivocally demonstrated the safety and efficacy of EVT in patients with large ischemic strokes based on parenchymal and perfusion imaging. 6-8,10,11 TESLA (Thrombectomy for Emergent Salvage of Large Anterior Circulation Ischemic Stroke) aligned with the results of the other trials but fell short of statistical significance (under review). 9

A post hoc subanalysis of RESCUE-Japan LIMIT (Recovery by Endovascular Salvage for Cerebral UltraAcute Embolism Japan-Large Ischemic Core Trial) 58 showed that EVT resulted in higher odds of survival with less disability compared with best medical therapy in patients with baseline ASPECTS of 4-5 (common odds ratio, 4.48 [95% CI, 2.07-9.71]) but no statistically significant evidence of clinical benefit noted with EVT in patients with baseline ASPECTS ≤ 3 (common odds ratio, 1.56 [95% CI, 0.79-3.10]) although, nominally, the association between ASPECTS and EVT benefit was in the same direction between patients with ASPECTS ≤ 3 and ASPECTS 4 to 5. Conversely, the magnitude of treatment effect was similar in ASPECTS 0 to 2 and ASPECTS 3 to 5 groups in both LASTE (Trial of Thrombectomy for Stroke With a Large Infarct of Unrestricted Size) and TENSION (EVT for Acute Ischaemic Stroke With Established Large Infarct). 8,10 In addition, the TENSION study showed no significant difference in mean infarct volume at 24 hours between patients undergoing EVT and medical therapy. 8 Although RESCUE-Japan LIMIT suggested a possible treatment interaction with ASPECTS occurring at an inflection point of 3, this could not be confirmed by a prespecified subgroup analysis from LASTE, which included a far greater number of patients, indicating the benefit of EVT that is similar to that seen in patients with small-to-moderate-sized cores and is present regardless of infarct size in patients who could be treated within 7 hours.

In an ANGEL-ASPECTS (Trial of Endovascular Therapy for Acute Ischemic Stroke With Large Infarct) prespecified subanalysis categorizing patients into 3 groups defined by ASPECTS and core volumes, the treatment effect did not significantly differ across the subgroups. 59 In SELECT-2 (Trial of EVT for Large Ischemic Strokes), the treatment effect of EVT persisted across all prespecified imaging subgroups, encompassing all ASPECTS scores, core volumes of ≥ 150 mL, and notably also in cases lacking a target mismatch profile. Furthermore, no treatment effect heterogeneity was observed in patients with a large core estimated by CT perfusion ( ≥ 70 mL) and a low ASPECTS (<6). These findings suggest that the benefits of EVT may extend up to 24 hours from symptom onset in patient populations exclusively composed of those with low ASPECTS, individuals with low ASPECTS and large perfusion core volumes, and even in patients with very small areas of reversible ischemia as defined by CT perfusion (penumbra). Although the TESLA 9 trial showed a trend toward benefit with endovascular treatment, the study narrowly missed the probability threshold for statistical efficacy. Nonetheless, no treatment effect heterogeneity was observed between patients with ASPECTS 2 to 3 and ASPECTS 4 to 5, nor was there a significant decrease in the size of the infarct volume or difference in ASPECTS score at 24 hours between endovascularly treated and medical groups. Although, formally, no treatment effect heterogeneity could be demonstrated in early (0-6) versus late (6-24) hour presenting patients, nominal differences in response to EVT were noted in these 2 groups of patients.

Across these studies, the treatment effect appears to persist across all imaging subgroups except possibly in late-presenting patients with ASPECTS <3. This challenges the conventional idea that existing imaging constructs can delineate patients for whom EVT might be ineffective or harmful, questioning the fundamental basis of imaging-based selection. Individual studies were not powered to allow definitive conclusions from subgroup analyses and, therefore, must be interpreted with caution as we await the results of individual pooled metaanalysis data. Despite these limitations, several speculations can be drawn to support our hypothesis.

First, in LASTE where more than half of the patients had ASPECTS 0 to 2 (in most cases by MRI), there was no difference in treatment effect compared with patients with ASPECTS 3 to 5. Despite the expectation of near complete or complete MCA territory involvement in ASPECTS 0 to 2, suggesting less penumbral volumes than in patients with small- or moderate-sized cores, the treatment effect remained robust and in the same range as in all other patients with proximal anterior circulation large vessel occlusion (numbers needed to treat, 4). If the benefit of reperfusion was exclusively occurring due to penumbral salvage, as currently ascertained by imaging studies in routine clinical care and, thus, proportional to the volume of mismatch, one would expect lower treatment effects with increasing core as the mismatch volumes diminish with increasing core (Figure 4). Nonetheless, in LASTE, a difference in follow-up infarct volume was noted between EVT and control patients, suggesting that even in patients with large infarct volumes, some reversible ischemic tissue (by volume) is still present and can be salvaged with reperfusion. Secondly, however, TENSION and TESLA showed similar follow-up infarction volumes between endovascular and medically treated patients, along with similar follow-up ASPECTS scores in TESLA. This contradicts the anticipated variability in final infarction volumes between EVT and control groups if reperfusion benefits were solely from penumbral salvage. Finally, in SELECT-2, nearly half of the patients had low CTP estimated penumbral volumes (<15 mL), yet the clinical benefit persisted. This aligns with a previous MR CLEAN subanalysis indicating persistent treatment benefits in patients without target mismatch profiles. Despite statistical limitations in using trials not explicitly designed to answer this question, these studies raise the possibility that salvageable penumbral tissue may exist within the confines of our radiographically estimated core, and a benefit of reperfusion may exist irrespective of the presence of imaging-defined penumbra.

In conclusion, both animal and human studies suggest that current neuroimaging methodologies, utilizing quantitative ADC, ischemic lesion hypodensity on CT, or CTP-derived perfusion thresholds, are not fully reliable in excluding microscopically salvageable ischemic tissue confined within the radiographically defined margins of ischemic injury. As these modalities lack the spatial resolution to detect the cellular biomarkers of potential ischemia reversibility, their validity in quantifying infarction depends on radiological-histopathologic correlative studies. Unfortunately, the overemphasis of early animal studies on the volumetric and macroscopic histopathologic features of infarction, rather than microscopic and molecular ischemic changes, contributes to the existing imaging-neuropathological gap of ischemia. This limitation is now being revealed by emerging data from the large-core EVT trials that demonstrated a treatment benefit of reperfusion that may exist irrespective of infarction volume, underscoring the drawbacks of relying solely on the volume of infarction, neglecting the underlying cellular and metabolic characteristics of ischemia that may greatly influence treatment response and functional recovery. Furthermore, recent studies suggest that diffusion restriction during acute focal ischemia may primarily represent increased astroglia volume, a compensatory and protective mechanism to regulate osmotic balance and shelter shrunken neurons from immediate osmotic injury (Figure 2). 40 Insights into glial osmoregulation could hold prognostic significance alongside infarction volume in acute ischemia and encourages the exploration of glial-targeted neuroprotective agents. Indeed, these imaging constructs may
(at best) predict the margins of infarction but cannot quantify nor distinguish between incomplete and complete infarction.

Current definitions of core and penumbra are likely limited by their oversimplification. First, considering the differential ischemic vulnerabilities between cell types (Figure 1), relying solely on a single hemodynamic marker such as CBF or early ischemic changes on CT may only predict infarction occurrence without accurately assessing the presence of viable tissue at a microscopic level within the ischemic core. 60 Recent models propose a more nuanced representation of this heterogeneity, suggesting the existence of minicores interspersed among minipenumbras. 61 Second, the static approach reduces the dynamic and interwoven metabolic, molecular, and cellular processes unfolding during acute ischemia, impacting both neurons and supporting structures. These processes encompass disruptions such as impaired mitochondrial ATP production, ionic imbalance, blood-brain barrier breakdown, aberrant cross-talk between brain innate and peripheral adaptive immunities, leukocyte infiltration, aggregation of activated platelets, upregulation of proinflammatory mediators, tissue remodeling and angiogenesis-related to matrix metalloproteinases, complement activation, glutamate excitotoxicity, and impaired nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidative pathways, among others. 62,63 Given the prognostic relevance of both early and delayed pathological changes alongside infarct size, reperfusion therapy may not only salvage the targeted penumbra but also attenuate the secondary injury cascade. Specifically, it may mitigate harmful processes such as glial transformation and neuroinflammation, which extend beyond the core and penumbra into surrounding tissue. This is crucial as neuroinflammation is linked to poorer functional outcomes and is mechanistically associated with neurocognitive decline and neuropsychiatric disorders. 64,65 Therefore, current core and penumbral constructs must be viewed in a fluid manner as dynamic entities for which the metabolism and function of the underlying cellular and molecular machinery are in constant flux and, in practice, provide unreliable information about tissue fate following reperfusion (Figure 5).

Recent expert opinions at the 12th Stroke Treatment Academy Industry Roundtable highlighted the absence of a specific core and penumbral volume that could determine treatment response following EVT, emphasizing the need for quantitative definitions of infarction. 66 Shifting from static and binary definitions to dynamic and quantitative ones may be essential for narrowing the imaging-neuropathological gap and defining imaging constructs with treatment-modifying properties. This may entail a multiparametric approach, by combining other relevant imaging parameters, such as collaterals and clot composition, with current or future imaging constructs. While these imaging variables are prognostically relevant, their ability to predict treatment response (in isolation) remains largely undefined. 67 If imaging is to remain a major factor in prereperfusion selection, next-generation imaging constructs should be merited by their ability to predict treatment response rather than prognosticate, irrespective of their pathophysiological validity. 12

Given the demonstrated safety and efficacy of EVT in large-core trials, the precision of future imaging constructs must be balanced against acquisition time. This may require the creation of separate imaging constructs: fast and practical for prereperfusion versus precise and granular for postreperfusion analyses. For instance, automated quantification of net water uptake on noncontrast CT in the emergency department (or even directly in the neuroangiography suite) could quantify prereperfusion infarction without significantly delaying treatment, while diffusible radiotracers can possibly enhance the hemodynamic precision of perfusion outputs. 53,68 Postreperfusion imaging may assist in individualizing neuroprotection, neuromodulation, and blood pressure augmentation in efforts to optimize reperfusion. 69 This may require disentangling the core by creating fingerprints of neuronal and astroglial responses using diffusion tensor imaging (as performed in recent neuroimmunological models) to stratify the diffusion signal and quantify the proportion of ischemic cell death to that of compensatory ischemic mechanisms. 70 In parallel, translational animal models should emphasize dynamic, voxel-based experiments that are conducted using quantitative perfusion measures, such as positron emission tomography or positron emission tomography magnetic resonance imaging (MRI PET), to quantify the molecular and microscopic neuropathological changes that occur within the macroscopic boundaries of infarction.

Anticipation surrounds the results of future metaanalyses that might help define the relationship between our imaging constructs and reperfusion outcomes. If future meta-analyses align with individual trials, indicating that none of our imaging surrogates, in isolation or combination, can effectively identify patients for whom EVT is ineffective or harmful, this supports the aggressive simplification of care systems. This shift from imagingbased selectivity toward speed and inclusivity raises a critical dilemma: how do we reconcile existing systems of imaging-based selection while acknowledging the profound limitations of current imaging constructs? Is the simplification in patient selection justified not only by faster reperfusion but also by the evident imprecision in our imaging constructs?

Our current imaging constructs have been critical in guiding us toward the forest but may have blurred the diversity of trees. Optimizing reperfusion therapies beyond mere recanalization will likely require entering and exploring the terrains of this uncharted territory. As we step into the era of precision medicine, we must reimagine our constructs by zooming in on the cellular and rebuilding them from the first-principal level. This journey must also be met with a psychological shift, as we must reconcile our desires for precision with the exquisite time dependence of treatment and the immense difficulty in predicting the behavior of complex biological processes. Nevertheless, continued efforts to narrow the imaging-neuropathological gap are critical to ensure that our diagnostics keep up with our therapeutics, in that our imaging constructs evolve and remain in stride with our reperfusion therapies.

segments.text: In acute stroke with a large ischemic region, endovascular therapy improved functional status at 90 d
Yoshimura S, Sakai N, Yamagami H, et al. Endovascular therapy for acute stroke with a large ischemic region. N Engl J Med. 2022;386:1303-13.
Question: In patients with acute ischemic stroke caused by large-vessel occlusion (LVO) and a large ischemic region, does adding endovascular therapy (EVT) to medical care improve clinical outcomes?
Design: Randomized controlled trial (RESCUE-Japan LIMIT [Recovery by Endovascular Salvage for Cerebral Ultra-Acute Embolism -Japan Large Ischemic Core Trial]).
Blinding: Treatment allocation concealed; blinded (outcome assessors, outcome adjudicators, data analysts, and data safety and monitoring committee).*

Patients: 203 patients aged ≥ 18 years (mean age 76 y; 56% men; median National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale [NIHSS] score 22) who had acute ischemic stroke, occlusion of the internal carotid or M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery, NIHSS score ≥ 6, Alberta Stroke Program Early Computed Tomographic Score (ASPECTS) value of 3 to 5, and modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score 0 or 1 before stroke onset; were randomized

within 6 hours of time last known well or 6 to 24 hours after last known well if there was no signal change in the initial image on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery; and for whom EVT could be initiated within 60 minutes of randomization. Key exclusions: clinically meaningful cerebral mass effect with midline shift, acute intracranial hemorrhage (ICH), or estimated high risk for hemorrhage.

Interventions: EVT plus medical care ( n = 101) or medical care alone ( n = 102). EVT could include stent retriever, aspiration catheter, balloon angioplasty, intracranial stent, and carotid artery stent and was selected by physicians. Medical care was consistent with guidelines from the American Heart Association and American Stroke Association.
Funding: Mihara Cerebrovascular Disorder Research Promotion Fund and Japanese Society for Neuroendovascular Therapy.
*See Glossary. Some information provided by authors.
Results : EVT + medical care vs. medical care alone in acute ischemic stroke caused by large-vessel occlusion with a large ischemic region

Commentary: Previous EVT trials underrepresent Asian populations, leaving uncertainty about the feasibility of mechanical thrombectomy in such patients with intracranial atherosclerosis -related LVO (1).

The trial by Yoshimura and colleagues showed that, in previously well-functioning patients with acute stroke and ASPECTS values of 3 to 5 in Japan, EVT improved outcomes vs. usual medical care alone. Included patients had large ischemic regions (less salvageable brain tissue and lower likelihood of a good outcome), whereas most previous trials excluded or had limited numbers of these patients. Although most EVT trials define a good outcome as an mRS score of 0 to 2 (2), patients with scores of 3 are still likely to have functional independence with similar quality of life as patients with scores of 2 (3).

Rates of post-EVT ICH increase in patients with larger regions of ischemic tissue (2). Although ICH occurred more frequently after EVT, groups did not differ for symptomatic ICH. Because EVT improved 90-day functional outcomes (number needed to treat = 6), rate of ICH in this trial is probably not important from a patient perspective.

Although guidelines recommend EVT for patients with ASPECTS ≥ 6 (4), this trial suggests more favorable outcomes with EVT in patients with a lower ASPECTS; EVT should be offered to patients who otherwise would not qualify for EVT with an internal carotid or M1 segment acute ischemic stroke.

Focused update to guidelines for endovascular therapy for emergent large vessel occlusion: large core and basilar artery occlusion patients
Steven W Hetts , 1 Fawaz Al-­ Mufti, 2 Guilherme Dabus , 3 Johanna T Fifi, 4 J Mocco, 5 Mahesh V Jayaraman 6

Endovascular therapy (EVT) dramatically improves clinical outcomes for patients with emergent large vessel occlusion (ELVO). Later this year, the Society of NeuroInterventional Surgery (SNIS) Standards and Guidelines Committee will update and supplement the existing SNIS guidelines on 'Embolectomy for stroke with emergent large vessel occlusion (ELVO)', 'Indications for thrombectomy in acute ischemic stroke from emergent large vessel occlusion (ELVO)', and 'Current endovascular strategies for posterior circulation large vessel occlusion stroke'. 1-3 However, given the importance of recent clinical trials in two specific populations with relatively common and devastating strokes, we summarize some of the new trial data and provide updated recommendations for treatment in a timely manner.
ANTERIOR CIRCULATION STROKES WITH LARGE ISCHEMIC CORE

Thrombectomy has been the standard of care for patients with anterior circulation ELVO and small to medium-sized ischemic cores (ASPECTS [Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score] scores 6-10 and core volumes <70 mL). However, recent trials, SELECT2, ANGEL-­ ASPECT, RESCUE-­ Japan LIMIT, and TESLA have challenged this previous limitation and demonstrated benefit to thrombectomy of the intracranial internal carotid artery (ICA) and M1

The Recovery by Endovascular Salvage for Cerebral Ultra-­ acute Embolism Japan Large Ischemic Core Trial (RESCUE-­ Japan LIMIT), 6 a multicenter, open-­ label, randomized clinical trial in Japan, randomized 203 patients with either CT or MR ASPECTS between 3 and 5, although MRI was primarily used for triage. The percentage of patients achieving a modified Rankin scale (mRS) score of 0 to 2 at 90 days was 14.0% in the EVT group versus 7.8% in the standard medical management group. The ordinal shift across the range of mRS scores favored endovascular therapy. Furthermore, the incidence of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH) was not significantly higher with EVT than with standard medical care.

The Randomized Controlled Trial to Optimize Patient's Selection for Endovascular Treatment in Acute Ischemic Stroke (SELECT2) trial enrolled 352 patients with large core strokes defined as ASPECTS 3-5 or CT perfusion-­ derived core volume >50 mL. 4 The patients were enrolled from the United States, Canada, Europe, Australia, and New Zealand to undergo EVT and receive standard medical care or to receive standard medical care alone within 24 hours since last known to be well. An interim analysis by the data and safety monitoring board recommended the cessation of recruitment. EVT was associated with a 90-­ day mRS 0-2 of 20% in the EVT group versus 7% in the standard medical management group. Rates of sICH were similar between the groups. Furthermore, EVT reduced by 50% the number of mRS 5 patients. 7

The Endovascular Therapy in Acute Anterior Circulation Large Vessel Occlusive Patients with a Large Infarct Core (ANGEL-­ ASPECT) trial randomized 456 patients in China with ELVO ischemic stroke patients and large core strokes defined as ASPECTS 3-5 but also core volume of 70-100 mL, presenting within

24 hours since last known to be well. 5 A planned interim analysis resulted in early termination on account of the 90-­ day mRS 0-2 of 30% in the EVT group versus 11.6% in the standard medical management group. Like SELECT 2, EVT reduced by 50% the number of mRS 5 patients. 7

The Thrombectomy for Emergent Salvage of Large Anterior Circulation Ischemic Stroke (TESLA) Trial was presented in May 2023 at the European Stroke Organisation Conference. While TESLA did not meet its primary intention-­ to-­ treat analysis of EVT superiority over medical treatment (90-­ day utility-­ weighted mRS), multiple secondary efficacy endpoints did favor EVT and its results were broadly in the direction of benefit for thrombectomy. 8 Specifically, EVT was associated with 90-­ day mRS 0-3 in 30% of patients compared with 20% of medically managed patients (p=0.03, OR 1.6). Similarly, major neurological improvement was 26% in the EVT group and 13% in the medical management group (p=0.0008). EVT treatment effect was smaller in TESLA (9.9%) as compared with RESCUE-­ Japan LIMIT (18.3%), ANGEL-­ ASPECT (13.7%), and SELECT2 (19.2%).

Also presented at the 2023 European Stroke Organisation Conference was a patient-­ level data meta-­ analysis of over 1000 patients from SELECT2, ANGEL-­ ASPECT, and RESCUE-­ Japan LIMIT. MAGNA (MechanicAl thrombectomy for larGe braiN infArctions) demonstrated meaningful improvement in mRS shifts (with good outcome defined as either mRS 0-2 or mRS 0-3) for patients with ASPECTS 3, ASPECTS 4, and ASPECTS 5 who underwent EVT. 9 This positive result was also evident for patients with ischemic cores of <70 mL (OR 1.97, 95% CI 1.27 to 3.05), 70-99 mL (OR 1.77, 95% CI 1.30 to 2.39), and 100-149 mL (OR 1.94, 95% CI 1.49 to 2.51). Only in the cohort of patients with ischemic cores of 150 mL or greater did EVT not demonstrate statistically significant benefit (OR 1.2, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.73).

Despite differences in design, methodology, and inclusion/exclusion criteria, all three published trials (SELECT2, ANGEL-­ ASPECT, RESCUE-­ Japan LIMIT) demonstrated benefits of EVT on mortality, severe morbidity (reducing the proportion of patients who survive with mRS 5 disability), as well as more traditional good functional outcomes (mRS 0-2). The results of these studies and the more recently reported but not yet published TESLA trial and MAGNA meta-­ analysis support the use of EVT for ELVO patients compared with standard medical management, thus warranting re-­ examination of our treatment guidelines. 1 2

In patients with anterior circulation ELVO who present within 24 hours of last known normal (LKN) with large infarct core and meet criteria of RESCUE-­ Japan LIMIT, SELECT2, ANGEL-­ ASPECT, or TESLA trials, thrombectomy is indicated (Class I, Level A).

Similar to the transition from IMS-­ III to the post-­ MR CLEAN era, new data in basilar artery occlusion strokes provide encouraging results regarding improved clinical outcomes. Although the randomized BEST (Basilar Artery Occlusion Endovascular Intervention versus Standard Medical Treatment) and BASICS (Basilar Artery International Cooperation Study) trials did not show a definite benefit of EVT over medical therapy, the newly published BAOCHE (Basilar Artery Occlusion Chinese Endovascular Trial) 10 and ATTENTION (Endovascular Treatment for Acute Basilar Artery Occlusion) 11 studies suggest that EVT within 12-24 hours of ictus is superior to medical therapy.

BAOCHE randomized patients with basilar artery stroke presenting within 6 to 24 hours after symptoms onset to EVT versus medical therapy. 10 Of note, although the trial was originally designed to have a good outcome designated as mRS 0-4, this was changed to mRS 0-3 after the trial was underway. After 110 patients received thrombectomy and 107 received medical therapy, the trial was stopped early at an interval analysis due to superiority of thrombectomy. Good outcomes were achieved in 46% of thrombectomy patients versus 24% of medical therapy patients (adjusted relative risk [ARR] 1.81, 95% CI 1.26 to 2.60, p<0.001) and sICH was uncommon but non-­ significantly higher in the thrombectomy group (6% vs 1%, RR 5.18, 95% CI 0.46 to 42.18). Mortality at 90 days was non-­ significantly lower in the thrombectomy group also (31% vs 42%, RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.04).

ATTENTION randomized basilar artery occlusion stroke patients within 12 hours of onset in a 2:1 manner to EVT versus best medical therapy. In total, 226 patients were assigned to the EVT arm and 114 to the medical therapy arm. 11 Good functional outcome defined as mRS 0-3 at 90 days was achieved in 46% of the EVT group versus 23% in the medical therapy group (ARR 2.06, 95% CI 1.46 to 2.91, p<0.001). Similar to BAOCHE, in ATTENTION the sICH rate was low overall but non-­ significantly higher in the EVT group (5%) compared with the medical group (0%). Mortality at 90 days was lower in the EVT arm (37%) than in the medical arm (55%, ARR 0.66, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.82). Of note, 14% of EVT cases were noted to have a procedural complication, including one death due to arterial perforation.
In patients with acute basilar artery occlusion who would meet criteria for BAOCHE or ATTENTION, thrombectomy is indicated (Class I, level B-­ R).
It is reasonable to consider thrombectomy for selected patients with basilar artery occlusion who do not strictly meet criteria for BAOCHE or ATTENTION (Class IIb, Level C).

In summary, we now have multiple randomized trials showing a benefit to thrombectomy in populations where previously there was a paucity of data. These results justify changes in local patient selection criteria for thrombectomy. Hub and spoke hospital systems should consider incorporating these results in determining which patients are appropriate for transfer to a center capable of performing thrombectomy.

abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: In this review, we summarize current evidence regarding potential benefits and limitations of using perfusion imaging to estimate presence and extent of irreversibly injured ischemic brain tissue ('core') and severely ischemic yet salvageable tissue ('penumbra') in acute stroke patients with large vessel occlusion (LVO). RECENT FINDINGS: Core and penumbra volumes are strong prognostic biomarkers in LVO patients. Greater benefits of both intravenous thrombolysis and endovascular therapy (EVT) are observed in patients with small core and large penumbra volumes. However, some current definitions of clinically relevant penumbra may be too restrictive and exclude patients who may benefit from reperfusion therapies. Alongside other clinical and radiological factors, penumbral imaging may enhance the discussion regarding the benefit/risk ratio of EVT in common clinical situations, such as patients with large core - for whom EVT's benefit is established but associated with a high rate of severe disability -, or patients with mild symptoms or medium vessel occlusions - for whom EVT's benefit is currently unknown. Beyond penumbral evaluation, perfusion imaging is clinically relevant for optimizing patient's selection for neuroprotection trials. SUMMARY: In an emerging era of precision medicine, perfusion imaging is a valuable tool in LVO-related acute stroke.

Does imaging of the ischemic penumbra have value in acute ischemic stroke with large
Pierre Seners a,b , Jean-Claude Baron b,c , Jean-Marc Olivot d and Gregory W. Albers e

In this review, we summarize current evidence regarding potential benefits and limitations of using perfusion imaging to estimate presence and extent of irreversibly injured ischemic brain tissue ( ' core ' ) and severely ischemic yet salvageable tissue ( ' penumbra ' ) in acute stroke patients with large vessel occlusion (LVO).

Core and penumbra volumes are strong prognostic biomarkers in LVO patients. Greater benefits of both intravenous thrombolysis and endovascular therapy (EVT) are observed in patients with small core and large penumbra volumes. However, some current definitions of clinically relevant penumbra may be too restrictive and exclude patients who may benefit from reperfusion therapies. Alongside other clinical and radiological factors, penumbral imaging may enhance the discussion regarding the benefit/risk ratio of EVT in common clinical situations, such as patients with large core -- for whom EVT ' s benefit is established but associated with a high rate of severe disability -- , or patients with mild symptoms or medium vessel occlusions -- for whom EVT ' s benefit is currently unknown. Beyond penumbral evaluation, perfusion imaging is clinically relevant for optimizing patient ' s selection for neuroprotection trials.
In an emerging era of precision medicine, perfusion imaging is a valuable tool in LVO-related acute stroke.
ischemic stroke, neuroprotection, penumbra, perfusion imaging, thrombectomy

In acute ischemic stroke (AIS), therapeutic trials have shown that the benefit of reperfusion therapies -either intravenous thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy - decreases as time elapses [1,2]. This observation is mostly due to the progression of the irreversibly injured ischemic brain tissue ('core') over time, at the expense of the severely ischemic yet salvageable tissue ('penumbra'): as time elapses and unless reperfusion is obtained, the penumbra proceeds to core until it has disappeared [3-5]. Importantly, the velocity of core growth over time - and its underpinning penumbra decrease - is highly heterogeneous across individuals [5,6 & ,7 & ]. Some patients, manifest large core and minimal penumbra within a very short time, while others still have small core and substantial penumbra several hours after symptom onset. Mapping the ischemic core and penumbra in AIS patients may therefore be of clinical interest to identify the patients who may benefit from reperfusion therapies.

In this review, we will discuss potential benefits and limitations of core/penumbra imaging for acute stroke patients. We will focus on patients with large vessel occlusion (LVO), where the core/penumbra model has been primarily studied.
